elements.text: Methylacrylate polymers with photochromic side chains containing heterocyclic sulfonamide substituted azobenzene
Ewelina Ortyl, Ryszard Janik, Stanisław Kucharski 米
Institute of Organic and Polymer Technology, Wroclaw Technical University, 50-370 Wroclaw, Poland Received 26 July 2001; received in revised form 25 January 2002; accepted 5 February 2002
Abstract

Methylacrylate monomers containing azobenzene groups with heterocyclic sulfonamide: sulfisomidyne (4-amino-N-[2, 6-dimethylpyrimidyn-4-yl]benzenesulfonamide) and sulfamethoxazole (4-amino-N-[5-methylisoxazol-3-yl]benzenesulfonamide) substituents were synthesized. The monomers were used for preparation of homopolymers and copolymers with butyl 2-methylacrylate and 2-ethylhexyl acrylate. The materials obtained showed photochromic properties manifested by trans–cis isomerization of the side chain azobenzene fragments induced by illumination with unpolarized and polarized light. The decrease of the absorbance of the EðtransÞ form at 450 nm was observed and the materials tested were in form of thin films deposited onto glass.

The isomerization of the polymers carried out during ellipsometric measurements showed the reversibility of the process in repeated illumination cycles with green laser light. The change of refractive index caused by illumination was in the range 0.005–0.008 as determined by ellipsometry.  2002 Elsevier Science Ltd. All rights reserved.
1. Introduction

Rapid development of nonlinear optics and optoelectronics in recent years has been connected with demand for storage and transformation of information. New materials which could increase density of information recording have been fabricated to replace inorganic materials used up to date [1,2]. Organic materials having photochromic and nonlinear optical properties have been of prime importance.

The molecule should have a proper structure to show photochromic and nonlinear optical properties. Its fundamental feature is the presence of an electron donor and an electron acceptor separated by the system of conjugated double bonds [1,3]. Such structure ensures acentrosymmetric distribution of electronic charge and relatively high diference of dipole moment of the ground and excited state of the molecule. The molecule placed then in an external electric or optic field is a subject to electronic charge movement causing a change of electron density, and a consequence of it, is a change of polarization state and an appearance of nonlinear optical properties [3,4].

Among materials containing chromophore groups the most promising seem to be polymers because their properties can be flexibly modelled. The chromophores can be placed randomly in a polymer matrix (guest–host structure), build into main chain or into side chain [1,3,5–7]. Interesting materials, considered as important ones in optical information recording and storage, can be methylacrylic polymers and copolymers containing azobenzene fragments in side chains [1,8–18]. The ability of the azobenzene group to reversible trans–cis (or E–Z) isomerization induced by light has been described in numerous papers [2,4,19–21]. Under illumination with visible or UV light, corresponding to absorption band, the more stable trans form undergoes tranformation to the less stable cis form. The reverse cis–trans reaction takes place as a thermal relaxation and it is relatively slow. To accelerate this transformation the illumination with light corresponding to the absorption band of the cis form is recommended [2,19–21]. The photoisomerization of the azobenzene group is particularly interesting because its consequence is a change of physicochemical properties of the materials such as: dipole moment, refractive index and dielectric permittivity, which can be interesting for practical applications in linear and nonlinear optics.

It was found that recording of information was dependent on anisotropy of polymers which could be achieved by orientation of polymer chromophore groups by action of linearly polarized light. This mechanism is based on the selective excitation of azobenzene groups whose dipole moment vector is placed in parallel position towards direction of light polarization plane [10]. These groups can undergo multiple isomerization trans– cis–trans cycles, but single excitation causes change of molecular orientation of the chromophores resulting in increase of concentration of these groups in direction perpendicular to the direction of polarization [2,18, 19,22,23]. The structure of the chromophore group is of prime importance, once by determination of the absorption band position, and twice, by facilitating or hindering the mobility of the side chain [10].

In this work we present synthesis of new chromophoric monomers, derivatives of azobenzene containing heterocyclic sulfonamide moieties. The monomers of the methylacrylate type contained aliphatic spacers (X) of diferent length between chromophoric and methylacrylic groups (Fig. 1). The monomers in question were polymerized to obtain homopolymers and copolymerized with butyl 2-methylacrylate and 2-ethylhexyl acrylate to get copolymers containing various percentage of chromophoric units. The aim of this work was to find relationship between structure, composition and kind of the macromolecular materials on glass transition temperature and ability to photoisomerization in thin polymeric films deposited on glass or silicon chips. The run of photoisomerization was investigated using UV-vis polarized and unpolarized spectroscopy and ellipsometry.
2. Experimental
2.1. Materials

Sulfisomidine, sulfamethoxazole were purchased from Aldrich, 2-[methyl(phenyl)amino]ethanol, 3-[methyl-(phenyl)amino]propanol, 2-{2-[methyl(phenyl)amino]- ethoxy}ethanol, 2-(2-{2-[methyl(phenyl)amino]ethoxy}- ethoxy)ethanol were obtained according to procedure described in [21].
The names of monomers according to IUPAC ACD/ Labs (Toronto) computer program, followed by SMILES notation (in parentheses), and symbols.

2.1.1. Synthesis of 2-[methyl(phenyl)amino]ethyl 2-methylacrylate (2a), 3-[methyl(phenyl)amino]propyl 2-methylacrylate (2b), 2-{2-[methyl(phenyl)amino]ethoxy}ethyl 2-methylacrylate (2c) and 2-(2-{2-[methyl-(phenyl)amino]ethoxy}ethoxy)ethyl 2-methylacrylate (2d)

2-[methyl(phenyl)amino]ethanol (0.17 mol, 25.3 g), 4- (dimethylamino)pyridine (2.1 g), and 4-methoxyphenol were dissolved in anhydrous pyridine (84 cm<sup>3</sup>) and methacrylic acid anhydride (0.22 mol, 34.0 g) was gradually added. The mixture was heated under reflux for 15 min. The solvent was removed with a rotary evaporator and a residue was dissolved in 100 cm<sup>3</sup> ethyl acetate containing 0.1 g 4-methoxyphenol. The solution was washed with 0.1 M aqueous $\mathrm { N a H C O } _ { 3 }$solution and with water and dried over anhydrous ${ \bf N a } _ { 2 } { \bf C O } _ { 3 }$. The solvent was then removed using a rotary evaporator. In this way the other title compounds were obtained. The yield was 77–98%.

The mixture of sulfisomidine (0.036 mol, 10.0 g), and concentrated HCl solution (18 cm<sup>3</sup>) was heated under agitation to 333 K, and 80 $\mathrm { c m } ^ { 3 }$of water and 118 cm<sup>3</sup> glacial acetic acid was added. The mixture was cooled down to 273–278 K and treated with small portions NaNO2 solution (0.043 mol in 7 cm<sup>3</sup> water) to keep temperature below 278 K. After 20 min the excess of nitric acid was removed with solution of amidosulfonic acid. Into this mixture, the cool solution of 2a (0.046 mol) in 150 cm<sup>3</sup> of 2-methoxyethan-1-ol was added under stirring and the temperature was kept below 278 K. Sodium acetate was then added (0.57 mol) and the mixture was kept overnight in a fridge. The reaction mixture was diluted with 3-fold amount of water, the solid precipitate filtered of and dried at 323–333 K. The product was purified by crystallization from dimethylformamide. The yield (of crude product) was 96%. 2.1.10. Synthesis of polymers and copolymers

The polymers and copolymers were obtained by radical polymerization of the monomers 2.1.6–2.1.12 in the presence of AIBN (10% by weight towards monomers). In a flask, the initiator and 5 g of monomer (and comonomer), in proportions shown in Table 2, was placed. The air was removed by passing nitrogen from the flask and a mixture of solvents: 30 cm<sup>3</sup> THF: cbutyrolacton ¼ 7:3 was added. The flask content was heated under reflux and ${ \bf N } _ { 2 }$atmosphere for 72 h. The reaction mixture was then poured into water and the formed precipitate was washed several times with fresh portion of water. The product was dried at 323–333 K.

The yield of polymers was 88–98%. Their structures was confirmed by <sup>1</sup>HNMR. The polymers of the IZO series showed signals characteristic for methyl groups in dimethylpyrimidine ring (2.3 and 2.4 ppm), methyl group at N atom (3.1 ppm) and protons at benzene ring (6.9, 7.9 and 8.0 ppm). Broad multiplets of methylene protons of nonchromophore mer (butyl 2- methylacrylate or 2-ethylhexyl acrylate) were visible at 1.0–2.0 ppm.

The polymers of the MET series showed signals characteristic for methyl group of isoxazole ring (2.34 ppm), methyl group at N atom (3.11 ppm) and protons at benzene ring $( \sim 6 . 9 , \sim 7 . 9$and 8.0 ppm).
2.2. Methods
The purity of the monomers and polymers was determined by thin layer chromatography using Merck Silicagel aluminium foils.
<sup>1</sup>H NMR spectra were made with 300 MHz BRU-KER Advance DRX-300 apparatus using CDCl<sub>3</sub> or DMSO-d6 solvent and TMS as an internal standard.
UV-vis spectra were made using Diode Array Hewlett Packard Spectrophotometer 8452 and quartz cuvettes of 1 cm spectral path.

Mean molecular weight of polymers was determined by GPC using Waters 917 columns, RIDK-102 detector and APEX ver.3.1 recorder. A mobile phase was c-butyrolactone and the molecular weight referred to polystyrene standards.
Glass transition temperature of the polymers was determined with a Mettler Toledo DSC. The temperature was programmed at 20 K/min.

The surface pressure isotherms were recorded with a home made Langmuir trough equipped with a NIMA PS4 sensor at 296 K. The samples were dissolved in $\mathrm { C H C l } _ { 3 } { : } \mathrm { D M S O } = 9 8 { : } 2$mixture. The evaporation time for the solvent was 30 min and the barriers were moved at a speed 5 mm/min.
3. Results and discussion
3.1. Syntheses

The methylacrylic monomers were obtained with very good yield of 93–98% by coupling of diazonium salt with intermediates 2a–d. The melting temperatures of the monomers were between 373 and 473 K (Table 1) and the monomers containing sulfisomidine heterocyclic ring (2,6-dimethylpyrimidin-4-yl) of the IZO-n series had higher m.p. temperatures as compared with corresponding sulfamethoxazole monomers (MET-n). In both homologous series, the m.p. temperature decreased with increasing length of aliphatic spacer joining nitrogen atom with methylacryloyl radical.

The molecular mass of the polymers determined by GPC was between 14 000 and 18 500, and it was rather low indicating that they were oligomers, what is in agreement with literature data [11,15]. The glass transition temperature $T _ { \mathrm { { g } } }$was in the range of 314–391 K. The $T _ { \mathrm { { g } } }$of homopolymers was higher than that of copolymers what was expected. Similarly, increasing length of the aliphatic spacer (X) in chromophore mer caused decrease of $T _ { \mathrm { g } }$[24]. Both incorporation of nonchromophoric co-monomer and increasing of the aliphatic spacer length were done to modify the physical properties of the materials in question. From one side, the content of the active chromophore was decreased but on the other hand, it was expected to reach better flexibility of the materials when subjected to molecular motion by influence of light.

The lowest $T _ { \mathrm { g } } = 3 1 4 . 7$K showed copolymer IZO-3/50 MB, having long aliphatic spacer chain and high content (50%) of nonchromophoric co-monomer. The copolymer IZO-1/80AI was a viscous oil at room temperature.
3.2. Photochromic properties of monomers and polymers

The UV-vis spectra were made for monomers and polymers in DMSO solutions. The maximum absorption band of both classes of materials was observed within wavelength in the range 440–460 nm (Tables 1 and 2). The position of the absorption band maximum of the monomers of sulfomethoxazole series (MET-n) lies at lower wavelengths, i.e. at 440–450 nm, whereas that of sulfisomidine series (IZO-n) is at 450–460 nm. Increase of the length of aliphatic chain in X spacer causes shift of the maximum absorption band towards longer wavelengths.

The trans–cis isomerization of the azobenzene group of the polymers in question was investigated for samples in form of thin films which were deposited on glass substrate by spin-coating from the solutions in THF (2– 2.5 wt.%). The UV-vis spectra of the films of selected

polymers before and after illumination with white light for 5 min were presented in Fig. 2. A decrease of the absorbance after illumination was caused by trans–cis isomerization of the azobenzene group resulting in an increase of the cis isomer content. The maximum absorption band of the latter was observed at 385 nm and was much weaker as compared with that of the trans form [20]. It was interesting that trans–cis isomerization was more enhanced in copolymers than in homopolymers what was probably caused by greater freedom of the chromophore group in copolymers to move during isomerization cycle. The UV-vis spectra were also made using polarized UV-vis beam for samples illuminated through polarization filter (Figs. 3 and 4). The distinct decrease of the absorbance was observed for the samples illuminated with p-polarized light and recorded with ppolarized beam but in the case of the same sample, in the spectrum recorded with s-polarized beam the decrease of the absorbance was considerably less pronounced. This indicates that there is an reorientation of the chromophoric groups in the films under influence of polarized light and that the domains are formed with increased content of the cis form [25].

elements.text: 3.3. Langmuir–Blodgett films

The side chain chromophoric groups are relatively long and they should form monolayer films on aqueous subphase. Determination of the run of surface pressure isotherms (P–r isotherms) of the polymers confirmed this presumption (Figs. 5 and 6). However, from observation of the isotherms run it results that the copolymers prevail over homopolymers. Incorporation of up to 20% of the nonchromophoric co-monomer improves the run of the isotherms making them steeper and this usually indicates that the film became more closely packed hence the collapse pressure exceeded 50 mN/m. Deposition of the L–B films onto a glass plate by vertical Y procedure was rather unsuccessful. The deposition degree was small and the film deposited showed tendency to slip from the glass plate. Horizontal deposition by so called ‘‘touch & carry’’ procedure made it possible to deposit monolayer onto glass plate and to get films containing up to 15 transferred monolayers. The films subjected to illumination showed similar efect of trans–cis isomerization as spin-coated ones, manifested by decrease of the maximum absorption band of the trans form. In this case, absolute values of absorbance and changes of it after illumination were smaller but still distinct.
3.4. Ellipsometric measurements

Ellipsometry is an optical method for measurement of thickness and optical parameters of thin layers by evaluation of polarization state of reflected light. The light interacts with the sample and undergoes a polarization change to elliptically polarized light. The change in polarization is measured as a ratio of the complex Fresnel reflection coeficients, $R _ { \mathrm { p } }$and $R _ { \mathrm { s } } ,$for p- and s-polarized light, respectively. The fundamental equation of ellipsometry is

where W determines intensity ratio and D determines the phase diference of the reflected p- and s-polarized light. From these measured values it is possible to calculate the film thickness and complex dielectric function expressed by complex refractive index:

$$
n = n _ {\mathrm{r}} + \mathrm{i} k
$$

The trans–cis isomerization of the azobenzene derivatives results in change of the dielectric properties of materials as cis-isomer formed has diferent dipole moment and molecular polarizability. The measurement of ellipsometric parameters before and after illumination with light showed distinct changes of W and D. The light source used in measurements was a green laser beam of 2 mm diameter and 3 mW power. The wavelength of the laser was 532 nm and this meant that it corresponded to the tail part of the chromophore absorption band. It is to mention that the wavelength of the laser built into the ellipsometer (measuring beam) was 632 nm. The illumination of samples on ellipsometer table with periodic switching light on and out showed that the process was reversible as presented in Fig. 7. The measured values of W and D served for determination of the thickness of deposited film and its refractive coeficients (real and imaginary) before and after sample illumination. Depending on the polymer, the change of real part of refractive index was between 0.0048 and 0.0071 (Table 3). The thickness of the deposited films was 300– 470 nm.
4. Conclusions

The methylacrylic monomers containing chromophore group could be easily obtained with over 90% yield by coupling reaction of diazonium salt of sulfisomidine or sulfamethoxazole with 2-[methyl(phenyl)- amino]alkyl 2-methylacrylates (alkyl ¼ 2a: ethyl; 2b: propyl; 2c: ethoxyethyl; 2d: (ethoxy)ethoxyethyl). The melting points of the monomers was between 373 and 463 K depending upon their structure.

Radical polymerization and copolymerization with butyl 2-methylacrylate and 2-ethylhexyl acrylate in the presence of AIBN as an initiator gave poly-molecular materials with average molecular mass in the range of 9900–18 500. The glass transition temperature of the polymers was between 315 and 391 K and decreased with increasing content of the nonchromophoric comonomer.

The trans–cis isomerization of the azobenzene side chain groups with polarized light formed domains in materials enriched with cis form. The observation of this phenomenon in ellipsometric measurements showed reversibility of the trans–cis–trans isomerization reactions. The determined change of refractive index during illumination with green laser light was in the range from 0.0048 to 0.0071. Therefore, the materials in question may be promising for information recording by holographic procedures.
